title: Hubble's view of dazzling globular cluster NGC 6397
caption: Globular cluster NGC 6397, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6397 · constellation Ara · about 7800 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and T. Brown and S. Casertano (STScI) Acknowledgement: NASA, ESA, and J. Anderson (STScI)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: Hundreds of thousands of stars glitter in this Hubble portrait of NGC 6397, an ancient globular cluster. Blue stars are scattered among them, a reddish glow comes from other stars, and a myriad of small white points fill the rest of the frame.

The colors reflect the stars' life stages. The blue stars are nearing the end of their lives. They have used up the hydrogen fuel that made them shine and now convert helium to energy in their cores, which burns hotter and makes them appear blue. The reddish glow comes from red giants, stars that have also run through their hydrogen and swelled in size. Many of the small white objects are stars like our Sun.

Astronomers used Hubble to measure the cluster's distance at 7800 light-years, making it one of the nearest globular clusters to Earth. The distance measurement was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.29 x 2.47 arcminutes) and distance (7800 light years), the frame spans roughly 7.5 × 5.6 light-years. Its light set out about 7,800 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue and red filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view picks out myriad individual stars, and the exposures gather far more light than an eye could.
